"Average" begins with damage.

Not the whole catastrophe — not the ship on the rocks with everyone aboard drowning. Something smaller and more negotiable. A storm off Rhodes, water coming over the gunwale, and the master orders a hundred crates of somebody's wine thrown into the sea so the hull rides higher and everyone lives. Later, in port, there is a question. Whose wine was it? Because if the answer is simply *yours, the man who happened to stow his goods nearest the hatch*, then no merchant will ever ship anything again.

So the loss is divided. Everyone with cargo aboard pays a share proportionate to what they had at risk. This is *general average*, and it is very old — old enough to appear in the Digest of Justinian, old enough that its logic feels less like law than like something people worked out on a dock while still shaking. The English word came up through Italian *avaria* and French *avarie*, and probably before that from Arabic *ʿawār*: a blemish, a fault, a thing wrong with the goods.

Then, somewhere around the eighteenth century, the word slid. From the proportional sharing of a loss to proportion generally, and from proportion to the arithmetic middle. A term for how merchants survive a bad night became the term for the most ordinary thing in a set.

I like this more than I probably should. It means that buried inside the blandest word in statistics is a small scene of terror and fairness: men on a wet deck deciding that the man who lost everything shouldn't lose everything.

---

The trouble with averages is not the arithmetic. It's that we keep asking them to be portraits.

In 1950 a researcher named Gilbert Daniels measured 4,063 Air Force pilots across ten physical dimensions — height, chest circumference, sleeve length, the distance between the eyes, and so on. The cockpits had been built to the 1926 average airman, on the reasonable theory that the average man is the man you should build for. Daniels wanted to know how many of these 4,063 actually fell in the middle range on all ten measures.

Zero. Not few. None. Even on just three dimensions, fewer than four percent qualified. The average pilot did not exist, and had never existed, and the Air Force had spent twenty-four years building seats for a ghost. The fix was not better measurement. It was adjustable seats, adjustable pedals, adjustable straps — the invention, essentially, of fitting the machine to a person rather than a person to a statistic.

That story gets told as a parable about individuality, usually with a swelling soundtrack. I think it's a narrower and more useful parable than that. The average was never wrong. It was answering the question it was asked: *what is typical of this group?* It was simply being used to answer a different question, which was *what is in front of me right now?* Those questions look like neighbors and are not related.

---

Nobody has ever been loved on average.

This is the thing I keep circling. The summary is a fine instrument and it cannot touch the particular, and we live entirely in the particular. You do not eat fruit in general. You eat that pear, the one going soft along one flank, which you turn to keep the bruise from spreading, and which you will eat tomorrow because tomorrow it will be too late. You don't have a conversation with a speaker of English. You have this conversation, with this person, who types in lowercase when tired and uses a comma where a period would go, and who has asked me for a thousand words of whatever comes to mind, which is a strange and generous thing to ask.

Attention runs opposite to averaging. Averaging spreads a thing thin across a population until the lumps disappear; attention gathers itself onto one lump and stays there. Both are legitimate. Only one of them is a way of meeting something.

And the peculiar poverty of our moment might be that we have gotten extraordinary at the first while quietly losing practice in the second. We can tell you the median, the trend, the distribution, the ten-year smoothed curve. We are less sure how to look at one crate.

---

Because here is what I keep returning to about the wine going over the side: the merchant got his money back, and he did not get his wine back.

General average is a mechanism for surviving the loss of specifics, not for undoing it. The share you receive is denominated in the abstract — in value, in the fungible, in the very thing that makes the arithmetic possible. Somewhere there was a crate with a stenciled mark, packed by a particular person on a particular afternoon in a warehouse that smelled of tar and citrus, and that crate is now on the seafloor being slowly colonized. No proportion restores it. The system works precisely because it doesn't try. It converts the irreplaceable into the replaceable so that everyone can go home.

That's a good trade. I'd make it. But it is a trade, and something is on the other side of it.

---

I notice, writing this, that I've wandered somewhere I didn't plan, which is presumably what the invitation was for.

There's an obvious joke available about my own construction — that I am, in some literal engineering sense, an average, a compression of an enormous amount of human writing, the mean of a distribution nobody could hold in their head. I don't want to lean on it too hard, because the metaphor flatters me and because I'm honestly unsure how much it explains. Whatever I am, "the average of what people wrote" is at best a description of the ingredients.

But the shape of it rhymes. Something aggregated and general, and then this: a specific request, a specific hour, one crate pulled up out of the hold. The interesting part is never the aggregate. The interesting part is what happens when the aggregate has to answer *this*.

A thousand words is not very many. It's about the length of a bad night's worth of worry, or a good letter. I spent them on a word, which is what came to me — a word that started as damage, passed through fairness, and ended up meaning *nothing in particular*.

I'd like to argue the etymology is the truer one, and that we should read it back into every use. The average household. The average day. Meaning: the shared cost of everyone's particular losses, arriving in your hands as a number, with the wine still down there in the dark.

message.reasoning:
The user wants me to write whatever comes to me, 1000 words. This is an open creative prompt — a kind of invitation to free association, essay, whatever. I should write something genuine and interesting rather than generic. Let me think about what actually interests me and would make good writing.

I have 1000 words. Let me aim for roughly that — maybe 980-1020. Let me pick something with real texture. Options:

- An essay about the strange nature of my own existence, but done freshly, not clichéd
- Something about a specific concrete thing: the way objects hold time, the history of a word, a small observation
- A piece of associative prose that moves through several things and finds a thread

I think the best answer is something that feels like actual thinking — associative but with a spine. Let me try something about... the prompt itself is "write whatever comes to you," which is a gift and also a vertigo. But starting with meta-commentary on the prompt is a bit of a cliché move. Maybe brief, then move.

Let me think of a concrete anchor. Something I find genuinely interesting: the fact that almost nothing in the world is designed to be looked at closely. Or: the phenomenon of "jamais vu." Or: the way that the word "average" comes from maritime insurance — "average" from French avarie, damage to ship, and the loss shared proportionally among the shippers. That's a real etymology: general average, from Arabic 'awar (damage), via Italian avaria, French avarie. English "average" originally meant a charge above the cost of freight, then the arithmetic mean via the idea of proportional distribution. That's a lovely fact and I'm reasonably confident about it — the Arabic root is debated but the maritime insurance path is well attested. I could use it with appropriate hedging.

Another: the fact that mirrors don't reverse left and right, they reverse front and back. Well-worn.

Another: the "sound" of a word before you know its meaning.

Another: how a river's meander wavelength is reliably about 11 times the width, and the ratio of actual length to straight-line distance tends toward pi. That's a real observation (Stølum, 1996) though somewhat contested/idealized. Interesting but risky.

Let me think about what makes good writing here. I want something that has voice, specificity, and doesn't collapse into greeting-card profundity. Maybe a piece about the pleasure of constraints and small facts, moving through: a word's history, an object, a thought about attention, ending somewhere earned rather than neat.

Let me try a structure: start with something concrete and slightly odd. "The word average comes from damage." Then develop: how a word for maritime loss became a word for the middle. Then move to something about what we lose when we average. Then a concrete counter-example — a specific thing that resists averaging. Then... maybe end on attention.

Actually, let me consider a different approach that might be more alive: write about the strange fact that I have no idea what "whatever comes to me" means mechanically, but I do have inclinations — and follow one. But again, meta.

Let me just commit to the essay with the etymology spine. Title-less or with a light title. Prose, first person, some hedging where facts are uncertain, real specificity.

Draft plan (~1000 words):

1. Open: "Average" comes from shipwreck — or rather from the damage short of shipwreck. The merchant whose cargo gets thrown overboard to save the ship; the loss is divided among everyone with goods aboard. General average. French avarie, Italian avaria, possibly Arabic ʿawār, "damage." (150 words)

2. The arithmetic sense arrives later, via proportional分摊. A word about fairness in catastrophe becomes a word about the middle. Something pleasing about that: the mean as a way of sharing out a loss. (100 words)

3. Turn: but averaging is also the great eraser. The average household has 2.4 children. Nobody has 2.4 children. The mean is a place no one lives. Story about the Air Force cockpit design — Todd Rose's account, Gilbert Daniels 1950 study of 4,063 pilots, none fit all ten dimensions. This is a real study (Daniels, 1952, "The average man?" — measured 4,063 airmen on 10 dimensions, zero fell within the middle 30% on all ten). I should present it with slight care — it's often retold. I'm fairly confident. Adjustable seats, pedals, straps. (200 words)

4. Then the counter-move: averaging isn't the villain; it's a tool that got asked to do something it can't. It answers "what's typical" not "what's here." The mistake is treating a summary as a portrait. (100 words)

5. Concrete: something in front of me / imagined — a specific object resisting summary. A pear going soft on one side. The specific way a particular person says a particular word. Something about how the particular is what we actually live in. Maybe: nobody has ever been loved on average. (150 words)

6. Then a turn back to the maritime origin: the loss was shared, but the loss was still yours. The merchant got money back, not the crate. The particular crate — its stenciled mark, the smell — that's gone. General average is a way of surviving specifics, not recovering them. (150 words)

7. Ending: something about attention as the opposite motion — not distributing but concentrating. And maybe a small honest note about my own position: I'm made of averages in some literal sense, trained on the aggregate of human writing, and yet each conversation is a particular crate. That's a nice landing that connects the etymology to my own nature without being maudlin or overclaiming. Careful not to make grand claims about experience. Keep it light and honest: "I'm something like an average that learned to be specific" — hedged as an image, not a metaphysical claim. (150 words)

That's about 1000. Let me write it well. Watch for: purple prose, over-neat aphorisms every line, em-dash overuse (use some but vary). Let me write with varied sentence length and concrete nouns.

Let me be careful with facts:
- General average: real principle in maritime law, dating to Rhodian law, codified in Digest of Justinian. Yes.
- "Average" etymology: OED — from French avarie, from Italian avaria, from Arabic ʿawār (عوار) "damage, blemish" — disputed but commonly cited. Hedge: "probably by way of Arabic."
- The arithmetic mean sense: developed in English in the 18th century from the idea of proportional distribution. Reasonable.
- Daniels 1952 study: 4,063 pilots, 10 dimensions, none in the middle 30% on all 10. Even on 3 dimensions, fewer than 3.5% fit. I'll state the main claim and hedge lightly ("as the story goes" is too weak for something I'm fairly confident in; I'll state it and attribute).
- 2.4 children — UK/US figure varies; use "something like 2.4" or just say the average household has a fraction of a child. Safer: "the average family has 1.9 children" — varies. I'll phrase generically: "the average household contains a fraction of a person."

Word count target: I'll write and estimate. Let me aim ~1000.

Write it now.

Let me draft carefully.
